what_it_does: When a large language model serves many users simultaneously, the GPU's expensive fast memory (HBM—the high-bandwidth memory chip stacked on the graphics card) fills up with each request's 'running notes' (the key-value cache, which stores the context each request has generated so far), limiting how many requests can be processed at once and leaving the GPU's compute units underused. NEO offloads some of those running notes and the attention math that reads them to the host CPU and its larger main memory, using a carefully designed pipeline that keeps both GPU and CPU busy simultaneously. The result is higher throughput with the same hardware at no accuracy cost.
method_in_detail:
The idea. The part of each transformer layer called 'attention'—where the model consults its running notes—is dominated by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic. A CPU's memory bandwidth is not that far below a GPU's bandwidth (200 GB/s vs. 600 GB/s for A10G), so the CPU can perform the attention step for a subset of requests in roughly the same time the GPU takes for other work. NEO exploits this to double-dip on hardware.

How it works. Each inference iteration is split into two asymmetric sub-batches. Batch-0 holds all new prompts being processed for the first time plus the majority of decode requests, and runs a long linear-projection phase (the heavy matrix multiplications where the GPU shines) on the GPU. Batch-1 holds a subset of decode requests whose running notes have been moved to CPU main memory; they run a long attention phase on the CPU. These two phases overlap in time: while the GPU crunches matrix math for batch-0, the CPU runs attention for batch-1 in parallel. New running notes created during the GPU's work are streamed to CPU memory layer-by-layer over the PCIe bus as they are computed, hiding transfer time behind GPU compute.

The key design choice. The batches are intentionally asymmetric rather than equal halves. Symmetric splitting (prior work) caused 'bubbles'—idle periods—because the GPU's linear stage and the CPU's attention stage are rarely the same length. By making batch-0's GPU linear stage deliberately longer (by bundling all new prompts into it) and batch-1's CPU attention stage the matching long side, both sides stay busy.

The scheduler. A load-aware scheduler runs every iteration, measuring estimated GPU and CPU compute times using offline-profiled lookup tables plus linear interpolation for unseen lengths. It greedily assigns requests to batches, comparing the estimated throughput of the asymmetric plan against a GPU-only plan and picking the better one.

The result. NEO achieves up to 7.5x higher throughput versus GPU-only on a memory-constrained T4 GPU, 26% gain on A10G, and 14% on H100, while maintaining the same per-request latency.
